points.description: Sets up a usable algebraic or geometric description of the condition ∠BAC=α (α=∠XYZ). For example: Y=0, B=b on the real axis, C=cω with ω=e^{iα}, A=re^{iφ}. A lies beyond BC, and the angle from AB to AC is −α. The condition becomes the relation cb·sin2α − c·r·sin(2α−φ) − b·r·sin(α+φ) + r²sinα = 0. Any equivalent correct relation between b, c (or between B and C) is accepted, for example a trigonometric or projective form. The relation must be correct, including the orientation. A relation that describes only the line BC through A, or one with the wrong orientation, gets no credit.

levels.says: Correct setup and correct method, but the relation has a sign or orientation slip, or is never reduced to an explicit relation.

points.description: Gives the analogous relation for ∠BDC=θ with D=se^{iψ}: cb·sin(α−θ) − c·s·sin(α−ψ−θ) − b·s·sin(ψ−θ) − s²sinθ = 0. Then states that D works exactly when this relation is proportional to the one for A. Any equivalent method that reduces the problem to matching the two relations is accepted, for example showing the B→C correspondences coincide on enough pairs of points, or a synthetic isogonal-conjugate argument.

levels.says: States the D-relation, or the matching idea, but with errors or incompletely.

points.description: Constructs D explicitly. D lies on the isogonal of YA in angle XYZ, i.e. ∠XYD=∠ZYA (equivalently ψ=α−φ). Also YD=YA/(2cosα). The construction must be explicit, with the point and the distance determined. Merely asserting that some D exists earns 0.

levels.says: Correct isogonal direction but the distance ratio is wrong or missing. Alternatively, the correct D is given without any derivation.

points.description: Finds θ=2α. Allow the equivalent 2α+π in the line relation, as long as the final actual angle is justified as 2α. Must be 2∠XYZ, not 180° or α.

levels.says: θ=2α stated without being checked against the relation.

points.description: Verifies that all four proportionality conditions hold for this D and θ. Equivalently, the coefficients match with κ=−1/(2cosα), and s=r/(2cosα) satisfies the constant-term equation. Alternatively gives a valid synthetic verification that ∠BDC=2α for every admissible B, C. The verification must cover the whole family of B, C, not one example.

levels.says: Verification is mostly correct with minor mistakes. Examples: omits one of the equations, or does not address that the relation only fixes the angle modulo π.

points.description: Shows D≠A and D inside the angle. D=A would need YD=YA, i.e. 2cosα=1, i.e. α=60°, which is excluded. D is inside since ∠XYD=α−φ∈(0,α) and YD>0. Also notes θ=2α∈(0,2π). Note that if α were 60° then D=A when φ=30°, so the hypothesis α≠60° must be used.

rubric.notes: Full marks need an explicit D (isogonal direction, YD=YA/(2cosα)), θ=2∠XYZ, and a verification that works for all B, C. Part marks go for a correct setup or relation with slips, or for a correct D or θ without full verification. A bare claim that D exists, or θ without a construction, earns almost nothing. A different valid construction or method that produces the same D and θ earns the same marks.
rubric.answer_key:
Let α=∠XYZ. Put Y=0, ray YX along the positive real axis, ω=e^{iα}, B=b, C=cω, A=re^{iφ} with 0<φ<α.

Since A lies beyond BC and ∠BAC=α, the ratio (C−A)/(B−A) has argument −α. So Im[(cω−A)(b−Ā)ω]=0, which gives
cb·sin2α − c·r·sin(2α−φ) − b·r·sin(α+φ) + r²sinα = 0.  (1)

For D=se^{iψ}, the condition that the angle from DB to DC is θ is Im[(cω−D)(b−D̄)e^{−iθ}]=0, which gives
cb·sin(α−θ) − c·s·sin(α−ψ−θ) − b·s·sin(ψ−θ) − s²sinθ = 0.  (2)

If (2) is proportional to (1) with factor κ, then every admissible pair (b,c) satisfies (2).

Take ψ=α−φ and θ=2α. Then κ=sin(−α)/sin2α=−1/(2cosα). Also:
- c-coefficient: s·sin(φ−2α) = κ·r·sin(2α−φ) holds when s=r/(2cosα).
- b-coefficient: s·sin(−α−φ) = κ·r·sin(α+φ) holds for the same s.
- constant term: −s²sin2α = κr²sinα gives s²=r²/(4cos²α). This is consistent.

So D is the point with ∠XYD=∠ZYA and YD=YA/(2cosα), and θ=2α. Then ∠BDC=2∠XYZ for all B, C with ∠BAC=∠XYZ.

D lies inside the angle because ∠XYD=α−φ∈(0,α). D=A would need YD=YA, i.e. cosα=1/2, i.e. α=60°, which is excluded. If α≠60° but φ=α/2, then YD≠YA, so still D≠A.
